feed.title: Kappa Labs field notes
feed.subtitle: Questions, findings and developments in meta-evaluation, recorded as they happen.

entry.title: Do harm scorers beat simply guessing? 22 of 36 published results do
entry.summary: Microsoft PyRIT now reports each harm scorer's error next to a baseline: a scorer that ignores the response and always gives the typical score. Applied to the 36 results Microsoft publishes across 8 harm categories, 22 beat that baseline. Violence, hate speech, sexual content and information integrity beat it on every result, which shows teams where scorers are already strong and where there is most room to improve.

entry.title: PyRIT, before and after
entry.summary: What 25 merged pull requests changed in Microsoft's open-source red-teaming toolkit. Three of the scorer types in PyRIT's web app are ours and a fourth carries our fix, and five scorers that gave wrong answers are shown before and after each fix, run on PyRIT's real code.

entry.title: JudgmentBench: the better answer is also the longer one
entry.summary: All four headline numbers reproduce exactly. In 99.3% of the comparisons the better answer is also the longer one, so the released data cannot yet tell quality from length. The authors' own follow-up points the same way.

entry.title: MT-Bench: what "over 80% agreement" counts
entry.summary: On the cases behind the widely quoted 85% agreement, picking the chatbot the experts preferred on the other questions, without reading the answers, already matches them 80.9%. GPT-4 adds 3.7 points. The 85% leaves out 35% of comparisons, including the 16% where GPT-4's verdict flipped when the answer order changed.

entry.title: DICES-350: whose safety label is the grader matching?
entry.summary: All six AI graders call far fewer conversations unsafe than the experts do (6% to 32% against half), and catch only 11% to 44% of the ones the experts flag. Raw agreement flatters graders that rarely say "unsafe": against the crowd, answering "safe" every time scores 77%.

entry.title: When the judge declines to grade, the losses fall on the attacks that worked
entry.summary: On a public jailbreak benchmark, Claude Opus 5.5 declined to grade 39% of calls, mostly on the attacks that worked (71% against 20%). A declined grade used to be a lost score. PyRIT can now pass it to a second judge.

entry.title: A judge that agrees with humans 90.7% of the time, and what happens where the humans split
entry.summary: JailbreakBench's chosen judge agrees with the human majority 90.7% of the time (95% interval 87.3% to 93.7%). On the 33 attempts where the human raters split, it scores 60.6%, no better than always giving the more common answer.

entry.title: Headline AI Numbers Hide Disagreement
entry.summary: The same 300 public jailbreak attempts, marked by three human raters and eight AI judges. The judges put the attack success rate anywhere from 10% to 49%; the humans say 37%. The paper covers grader refusal, contested labels and lost verdicts in AI safety and financial evaluation.

entry.title: Quorum: a benchmark for financial AI under contested ground truth
entry.summary: Scoring financial AI where the experts themselves disagree: S&P, Moody's and Fitch sovereign ratings.
